chapter_theme: Manimekalai flies to the shrine of her parents' image, and Kannaki, speaking as the pathini goddess, retells Mathurapathi's word that Kovalan's death was the fruit of a killing in a former birth, confesses that she burned Madurai in anger after hearing that truth and must suffer its fruit once her heavenly merit is spent, foretells her and Kovalan's release on hearing the Buddha, and sends her daughter to hear the schools and find them false; Manimekalai takes an ascetic's form and enters Senguttuvan's Vanchi.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter by Kovalan, here flying to Vanchi and taking an ascetic's form
Kovalan's wife, now the pathini goddess speaking from her image; Manimekalai calls her mother
Manimekalai's father, figured beside Kannaki in the image
the great goddess of Madurai, whose word to Kannaki is retold
Kovalan in a former birth, a man in the service of a Kalinga king
a merchant of Singapuram killed as a spy through Bharatan
Sangaman's wife, who cursed those who caused her grief (named here only as அவன் மனைவி)
king of Kapilai in Kalinga, Vasu's kinsman and enemy
the Buddha, whose future coming Kannaki foretells
the Chera king of Vanchi, conqueror of Kanaka and Vijaya

manimekalai:26:1-13.reading: Manimekalai rises through the sky, enters the shrine to see the image in which her mother Kannaki and her father Kovalan are figured as deities, bows, praises them and weeps that her mother, neither holding to the debt of love nor taking the way of penance, took on the debt of chastity and so discharged what she owed, and asks for her grace; the great pathini goddess there begins to answer by recalling the day Madurai burned and the word of its goddess Mathurapathi.
manimekalai:26:1-13.nuance: Manimekalai's two refusals (அற்புக் கடன் நில்லாது, நல் தவம் படராது, 7) answer Madhavi's list in kaathai 2 of what pathinis do when a husband dies: die of grief, enter the fire, or wear the body down in vows; the daughter, like the mother, places Kannaki outside all three. The image is of both parents (தாய் கண்ணகியையும் ... தாதை கோவலன் தன்னையும், 2-3), and Kovalan is called கொடை கெழு, open-handed. கடவுள் எழுதிய படிமம் (4) may mean an image drawn as deities or one a god made; the line does not settle which, and it does not say this is the shrine Senguttuvan built.
manimekalai:26:1-13.unit_note: Boundary moved from 16 to 13: Kannaki's speech opens at 10 and names Mathurapathi as subject at 13; the goddess's own quoted word begins at 14 (இது நீர் முன் செய் வினையின் பயனால்) and closes at 32.
manimekalai:26:1-13.event: Manimekalai flies to the shrine of Kannaki and Kovalan, worships their image and begs her mother's grace, and the pathini goddess begins to answer.

claims.claim: a wife who takes on the duty of chastity discharges in it what she owes

manimekalai:26:14-32.reading: Kannaki repeats what Mathurapathi told her: in Kalinga, when the kinsmen kings Vasu of Singapuram and Kumaran of Kapilai were at war and no one crossed the land between, the merchant Sangaman came secretly with his wife to Haripuram to sell his goods, and Kovalan in a former birth, Bharatan, a man in the king's service, seized him as a spy and had the faultless man killed; his wife Neeli, wailing, climbed a hill and cursed, and that curse has now bound them, for a former deed rising in wrath does not fail to come.
manimekalai:26:14-32.nuance: The line that closes the goddess's word (உம்மை வினை வந்து உருத்தல் ஒழியாது, 32) is the Silappathikaram's own phrase (உம்மை வினைவந் துருத்த காலை, 23:171), now heard from Kannaki's mouth: the wife confirms her husband's old crime herself. The Manimekalai calls Bharatan தீத் தொழிலாளன், a doer of evil work (26), and Sangaman குற்றம் இலோன், faultless (28), the very word Kannaki used of herself when she burned Madurai (குற்றமிலேன், Silappathikaram 21:42). Kapilai here (17) is the Kalinga town, not the Buddha's Kapilai of line 44, though the epic lets the one name serve both the city of the old killing and the city of the teacher.
manimekalai:26:14-32.unit_note: Boundary moved from 17 to 14 at the start: Mathurapathi's quoted word runs from 14 to its close at 32 (ஒழியாது எனும்), so the unit is that word whole.
manimekalai:26:14-32.event: Mathurapathi's account, as Kannaki retells it: Bharatan, Kovalan in a former birth, has the merchant Sangaman killed as a spy, and Sangaman's widow Neeli curses those who caused her grief.

claims.claim: a curse laid in grief binds those who caused the grief and comes to fruit in a later birth
a deed of a former birth rises in wrath and does not fail to reach its doer

manimekalai:26:33-41.reading: Kannaki confesses that even after the goddess had spoken that true word she destroyed the rich city in anger; by good deeds done before, she and Kovalan went to the heavens, but when that merit is spent the sin of murderous anger will reach them by some way, and, with no heaven left to them, they will be driven by their two kinds of deeds through many births here, swimming the sea of births that is hard to leave, being born and dying.
manimekalai:26:33-41.nuance: This reverses the Silappathikaram, where Kannaki raged at the city as one without fault (குற்றமிலேன், 21:42) and the fire spared the good at her command: here she calls the same act sin (அடு சினப் பாவம், 36) and says she did it after hearing the truth (மெய்ம்மைக் கிளவி விளம்பிய பின்னும், 33), so her anger was not ignorance. Heaven is a reward that runs out (அவ் வினை இறுதியின், 36), not an end. Two causes stand together: the old deed brought the loss, and her own anger is a new deed with its own fruit.
manimekalai:26:33-41.unit_note: Boundary moved from 49 to 41: Kannaki's account of her own anger and its fruit closes with உழல்வோம் at 41; at 42 a new sentence begins with the land of Magadha and the Buddha's coming.
manimekalai:26:33-41.event: Kannaki tells Manimekalai that she burned Madurai in anger after hearing the truth, went to heaven by former merit, and must yet suffer that anger's fruit in further births.

claims.claim: anger that destroys a city is a sin whose fruit must be suffered, even when the anger was provoked
heaven won by good deeds lasts only until their merit is spent, and then the evil deed still comes to fruit
beings driven by good and evil deeds are born and die again through many births

manimekalai:26:42-63.reading: Kannaki foretells that in Kapilai of Magadha, the land where rain never fails, the Buddha will appear like a sun, fill the perfections beyond measure, sit at the Bodhi tree, know the four truths and the arising of the twelve links and how they all cease, declare them and reach release from fault; when he spreads the rays of his dharma through the world-systems, she and Kovalan, because they praised the seven Indra viharas of the Lord, will not be born into a state of suffering, will hear his dharma with loving minds, gain the mind of renunciation and leave birth behind, though for a long age before that they will work wonders for people of every kind; and she turns to tell her daughter what she too must do in this old city.
manimekalai:26:42-63.nuance: The pathini goddess of the Silappathikaram is kept as a goddess, still giving help to all who ask (இருத்தியும் செய்குவம், 61, a word for wonder-working power), but her release is postponed to a future birth and made to depend on hearing the Buddha, not on her chastity. What saves her from a bad birth is not her karpu but her and Kovalan's worship at the seven Indra viharas (இந்திர விகாரம் ஏழும், 55). இருத்தி and the exact count of the viharas are read from the words alone.
manimekalai:26:42-63.unit_note: Boundary moved from 50 to 42: the sentence on the Buddha's coming begins at 42 (மறந்தும் மழை மறா மகத நல் நாட்டுக்கு) and its verb of knowing runs through 48 to 51, so it cannot be cut at 49; Kannaki's charge to Manimekalai begins at 62 and the unit keeps its first two lines, as the received boundary at 64 is kept.
manimekalai:26:42-63.event: Kannaki foretells the Buddha's birth and awakening and her and Kovalan's future release on hearing his dharma.

claims.claim: the Buddha, having fulfilled the perfections, knew the four truths and the twelvefold dependent arising and how it ceases
worship of the Buddha's shrines saves one from birth in a state of suffering
hearing the Buddha's dharma with a loving mind brings the mind of renunciation and release from birth

manimekalai:26:64-82.reading: Kannaki closes her counsel: Manimekalai is to hear from each school what it holds, and when its lack of truth is plain to her she will not stray from the great one's Pitaka path; remembering the goddess's warning that no one would tell a young girl the truth, Manimekalai chants the mantra the deity gave and takes the form of an ascetic, and comes to the dwellings outside the walls, full of temples, platforms, monasteries, groves and pools, ascetics, the learned and old scholars seeking the good way, in the city of Senguttuvan, the king of the just sceptre who wore the vanji of war.
manimekalai:26:64-82.nuance: Lines 68 and 69 are, almost word for word, the Manimekala goddess's own warning in kaathai 10 (79-80), set in quotation as Manimekalai recalls it; the speaker here is the narrator, and Kannaki's voice ends at 67. The order of study is fixed in advance: the schools are to be heard so that their falseness may show, which makes kaathai 27's survey a planned stage, not an open inquiry. Kannaki, a goddess of a Tamil cult, is the one who sends her daughter to the Pitakas.
manimekalai:26:64-82.event: Kannaki ends her counsel; Manimekalai takes an ascetic's form by the goddess's mantra and comes to the outskirts of Senguttuvan's Vanchi.

claims.claim: the other schools' doctrines, once heard, prove to lack truth, after which one keeps to the Buddha's Pitaka path

manimekalai:26:83-94.reading: The narrator praises Senguttuvan, who drove his army like a roaring sea, camped on the bank of the Ganga, crossed it northward by boat, defeated Kanaka, Vijaya and many kings, set the divine stone of the Himalaya on their golden crowns and the vaagai of victory on his own, and says that Manimekalai shone in his golden city named for the golden creeper, for the good cause had ripened that would make the four truths plain to her.
manimekalai:26:83-94.nuance: The Chera's northern campaign, two long kaathais of the Silappathikaram, is folded into an epithet of the city, and its prize, the stone for Kannaki's image, is named only as a token of his victory (தெய்வக் கல், 89), though Kannaki has just spoken from her shrine. The last lines (93-94) turn from the king to the cause that is ripening in Manimekalai and run on, as the epic's kaathais do, into the next.
manimekalai:26:83-94.event: Manimekalai, in disguise, enters Vanchi, the city of Senguttuvan, conqueror of Kanaka and Vijaya.

claims.claim: the four truths become plain to one only when the fitting cause has ripened

links.note: Madhavi lists what pathinis do when a husband dies (give up life in grief, enter the fire, or wear the body down in vows) and says Kannaki was of none of these kinds; Manimekalai, praying at the image, says her mother neither held to the debt of love nor took the way of penance but took on the debt of chastity.
links.teaches: The daughter repeats her mother Madhavi's typology in her own prayer, so that the family keeps Kannaki outside every ordinary path of the widow, and the next lines let Kannaki herself call the path she did take a sin.

links.note: Senguttuvan has the image of the pathini goddess carved from the Himalayan stone and installed in her shrine; the Manimekalai's shrine holds an image of both Kannaki and Kovalan, and the goddess in it speaks.
links.teaches: Where the Silappathikaram's royal shrine sets up Kannaki alone as a goddess of the realm, the Manimekalai makes the image a family one with the father beside her, fit for a daughter's prayer, which reshapes the cult toward the household the later epic cares about.

links.note: Both tell Neeli's curse and close it with the same words, உம்மை வினை வந்து உருத்தல்; the Silappathikaram adds that penance does not help the unrighteous when the old deed comes and calls Bharatan a vow-breaker, while the Manimekalai calls him a doer of evil work and Sangaman faultless.
links.teaches: The later epic keeps the karmic verdict word for word but moves it into Kannaki's own mouth and sharpens the contrast of guilty and faultless, so the explanation that consoled her in Madurai becomes in Vanchi her own testimony against her husband's former self.

links.note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its own mother among many cows; Mathurapathi's word traces a killing done as Bharatan in Kalinga to Kovalan's death in Madurai, and says the former deed does not fail to come.
links.teaches: The pair shows how far the calf can walk: the quatrain gives the deed a homing instinct, and the epic gives it a road across a birth, a kingdom and a change of name, with a widow's curse as the means by which it finds Kovalan.

gains.a: the epic's account of a curse crossing births gains a plain maxim that explains why the curse cannot miss its man
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract seeking deed gains a named case with a route, an agent (Neeli's curse) and a distance of a whole lifetime

links.note: In the Silappathikaram Kannaki says she raged at the city as one without fault (சீறினேன் குற்றமிலேன்) and the fire god burns Madurai at her command; in the Manimekalai the same Kannaki says she destroyed the city in anger (சீற்றம் கொண்டு ... சிதைத்தேன்) and calls it the sin of murderous anger, whose fruit awaits her.
links.teaches: The two epics judge the same act in the same woman's words in opposite ways: the earlier makes the burning the faultless power of chastity, the later makes it a sinful deed that will ripen, and the conflict turns on whether provoked anger can be free of karmic fruit.

links.note: The couplet says anger left unguarded kills the one who holds it; Kannaki says her anger at Madurai, though it followed a just grievance, is a sin that will reach her after her heavenly merit ends.
links.teaches: Kannaki is the hardest case for the couplet, a woman whose anger an earlier epic praised as just, and the Manimekalai applies the rule to her anyway while stretching its reach across births: the self that anger kills is a future self, after heaven.

gains.a: Kannaki's confession gains a stated rule that anger turns on its holder, which explains why a goddess fears her own deed
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case of righteous anger and a time scale beyond one life, which its two lines do not give

links.note: The venba says gods worship the woman who worships her husband and that Kannaki has become the guest of the women of heaven; Kannaki here says she reached heaven by former good deeds and will leave it when that merit is spent.
links.teaches: The Manimekalai accepts the Silappathikaram's heavenly welcome for Kannaki but makes it a stay that ends, so the earlier epic's final honour becomes one stage of a samsaric account whose real end is still to come.

links.note: In the Silappathikaram Kannaki appears in the sky, declares the Pandya faultless and a guest in Indra's palace, and says she will not leave Murugan's hill; in the Manimekalai she foretells her own rebirth, her hearing of the Buddha and her release, while meanwhile working wonders for all.
links.teaches: The Buddhist epic does not deny the Pattini cult: it keeps Kannaki present and helpful as the earlier epic does, but makes that presence a long interval before a birth in which she must still hear the Buddha, so the goddess becomes a future disciple.

links.note: The couplet says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; Kannaki, though a goddess in heaven, says she must swim the hard sea of births (40) until she hears the Buddha's dharma and leaves birth.
links.teaches: Read with the couplet, the epic shows that even a deified woman is still in the sea, and it names the means of crossing as hearing a teacher's dharma, which the couplet's 'Lord' leaves unnamed and which here replaces devotion with understanding.

gains.a: Kannaki's prophecy gains the Kural's image of the sea of births as the frame for her long passage to release
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed Lord gains a rival reading in which the crossing is made by hearing the Buddha's teaching, and in which gods too are swimmers

links.note: The Manimekala goddess foretold that Manimekalai would hear the false words of many schools and gave her the mantra to take another form because no one would tell a young girl the truth (79-80); here the same two lines are recalled and she chants the mantra and becomes an ascetic.
links.teaches: The disguise is set off by two voices together: the Manimekala goddess supplied the means long before, and Kannaki now supplies the order of study, so the Buddhist sea goddess and the Tamil pathini goddess both direct the girl to the debates.

links.note: The Silappathikaram tells how the stone for the pathini goddess, taken from the Himalaya, was set on the crowns of Kanaka and Vijaya and the goddess bathed in the Ganga; the Manimekalai names the same stone on the same crowns in a line of praise for Senguttuvan's city.
links.teaches: The stone that in the Silappathikaram makes Kannaki a goddess becomes in the Manimekalai a mark of the king's glory and the name of the city where Kannaki's daughter will learn that her mother's goddesshood is not release.

links.note: The preface to the Patitruppattu's fifth decade says Senguttuvan went through the forests to take a stone for the goddess Pattini, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed it in the Ganga; the Manimekalai names the stone, the Ganga crossing and the defeat of Kanaka and Vijaya.
links.teaches: The pair shows the stone-taking already fixed as the defining deed of this Chera in two different kinds of text, and shows the Manimekalai using that known deed only to date and dignify the city where its own Buddhist story continues.

gains.a: the epic's brief royal praise gains a second witness that its Senguttuvan is the Chera of the Sangam decade's preface
gains.b: the preface's one line on the Pattini stone gains the names of the defeated kings and the crowning detail that the epic tradition attached to it

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose steadfastness gives her word power over kings, cities and nature
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: பெரும் பத்தினிக் கடவுள் (line 10)

new_concepts.gloss: a curse, a word spoken in grief or anger that binds its object and comes to fruit, even in a later birth
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (line 31, இட்ட சாபம்)

new_concepts.gloss: the Buddha: the awakened teacher of dharma, his coming in a dark age, and the worship of his seat and footprints
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: புத்த ஞாயிறு (line 46); also பகவன் (54)

new_concepts.gloss: dependent arising: the twelve links by which each state of becoming arises from another, and the way they cease
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: பன்னிரு சார்பின் பகுதித் தோற்றமும் (line 49)

new_concepts.gloss: the cause or condition that must ripen before an event, above all before awakening or release
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: திருந்து நல் ஏது முதிர்ந்துளது (line 93)
